title: Three kinds of knowledge, action, doer (18.19–18.28)
hook: the Gita sorts how you see, what you do, and who you are while doing it

segments.voice: Yesterday: daiva, five causes of action. The seat, the doer, the instruments, the efforts, and the unseen fifth. Your line was not I alone. Did you name another cause today? Now, the three threads, one more time. Day two hundred twenty-one.

Three people get the same assignment. One looks at it and sees how it fits into something larger. One sees only their own part, and fights to protect it. One grabs a single detail, decides that's the whole thing, and stops thinking. Same task. Three ways of seeing it. Then they do the work: one steadily, one frantically, one carelessly, putting it off. The Gita has been building to this. Yesterday it counted the causes of action. Today it sorts the knowing, the doing and the doer by the three threads.
screen: `SAME TASK, THREE PEOPLE.` → `THE WHOLE, A PIECE, ONE DETAIL.` → `STEADY, FRANTIC, CARELESS.`

segments.voice: Knowledge first. Verse twenty: sattvic knowledge sees one undying reality in all beings, undivided in the divided. You've heard that before; it's chapter thirteen's one light. Verse twenty-one: rajasic knowledge sees all beings as separate, each its own thing, nothing connecting them. Verse twenty-two: tamasic knowledge clings to one small piece as if it were everything, without reason, without grasping what's true. Then action. Verse twenty-three: sattvic action is what needs doing, done without attachment, without craving or hate, by someone not chasing the fruit. Verse twenty-four: rajasic action is driven by desire or ego, done with enormous strain. Verse twenty-five: tamasic action starts in confusion, with no thought for the consequences, the loss, the harm to others, or even whether you're able. Then the doer. Verse twenty-six: the sattvic doer is free of attachment, doesn't talk about themselves, is full of steadiness and energy, and unchanged by success or failure. Verse twenty-seven: the rajasic doer is passionate, wants the fruit, is greedy, can be harmful, and swings between joy and grief. Verse twenty-eight: the tamasic doer is unsteady, crude, stubborn, deceitful, lazy, gloomy, and dirghasutri. That last word is a compound of dirgha, long, and sutra, thread. Long-threaded: someone who keeps stretching a job out. A procrastinator. So a word for putting things off is sitting in the Gita's last chapter. The chapter goes on to sort understanding, resolve and even happiness the same way. The point isn't to label yourself forever. It's to see which kind you're being right now. That's the word today: three kinds of knowledge.
screen: `SEEING ONE, SEEING MANY, SEEING A BIT.` · `STEADY, STRAINED, OR CARELESS.` · `THE DOER UNCHANGED BY SUCCESS.` · `DIRGHASUTRI: THE PROCRASTINATOR.` · then, large: `THREE KINDS OF KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one task waiting for you. Notice how you're seeing it. As part of something bigger? As only your piece? As one annoying detail? Then notice how you'd do it: steadily, frantically, or not at all yet. No judgment. Now picture yourself doing it the steady way, with energy but without needing praise. Hold that picture for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.

Dirghasutri, long-threaded, one who drags a task out. Gita eighteen, nineteen to twenty-eight: knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the tamasic doer is dirghasutri.
Your line: know your kind. Today, pick the one task you've been stretching out, and do the first steady piece of it. Day two hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 18.19–18.28 as a mirror for work and study: aiming for sattvic knowledge, action and doing, steady, unattached and unshaken by success or failure.

match.prompt: three kinds each — tap the pairs.
pairs: one piece taken for the whole

myth: the sattvic doer is unchanged by success or failure
verse 26: steady, energetic, free of attachment and self-talk.
the Gita praises action done with enormous strain as the highest
verse 24: action driven by desire or ego, with great strain, is rajasic.
the Gita has a word for procrastinator

fork.setup: you see that everyone on your team is part of one project, and you do your part without needing credit. which kind is that?
fork.reveal: sattvic: seeing the one in the many (verse 20), and acting without attachment to the fruit (verse 23).

original.note: Sanskrit: dirghasutri, long-threaded (dirgha, long + sutra, thread): the one who drags a task out; Gita 18.28.

trapdoor: what you thought: the three kinds are about good and bad people.
what it means: knowledge, action and the doer can each lean clear, restless or heavy, and you can notice which one you're being now.
what a scholar hears: 18.20 'avibhaktam vibhakteshu', undivided in the divided; 18.28 lists 'dirghasutri' among tamasic traits; 18.29–18.39 extend the scheme to buddhi, dhriti and sukha.

notes: The outline skips 18.29–18.40 (understanding, resolve, happiness); the script mentions them in one line as a bridge to day 222.
